sidebar: An interactive apologetics codex across Islam, Judaism, Hinduism & Sikhism — Volume 1 of the comparative series, complete at 100 questions per tradition.
preface: This book is written from a Christian perspective, but it aims to represent other traditions accurately and charitably before offering a Christian response. The goal is persuasion through honesty, not mockery. Two rules govern every entry in this book:

Each entry follows the same structure: Context, the mainstream position with primary sources, a Christian apologetic response, and points for respectful discussion — because a debate opponent who feels straw-manned will not listen, no matter how strong the argument is.

A note on hadith grading: hadith are classified by Muslim scholars themselves as sahih (authentic), hasan (good), da'if (weak), or mawdu' (fabricated). Where a hadith's authenticity is disputed, that is noted — using a weak or fabricated hadith as if it were authoritative is a common and easily-refuted mistake in amateur apologetics, and this book avoids it.

The following questions are among the most common raised in Christian–Muslim dialogue and formal debate (e.g., exchanges associated with debaters such as Jay Smith, David Wood, Nabeel Qureshi, Yasir Qadhi, and Shabir Ally). They are presented here in their strongest, most defensible form — sensationalized versions of these questions exist online and are easily dismissed by informed Muslim respondents, which only weakens the Christian debater's credibility.

islam.title: Islam
islam.lead: The following questions are among the most common raised in Christian–Muslim dialogue and formal debate (e.g., exchanges associated with debaters such as Jay Smith, David Wood, Nabeel Qureshi, Yasir Qadhi, and Shabir Ally). They are presented here in their strongest, most defensible form — sensationalized versions of these questions exist online and are easily dismissed by informed Muslim respondents, which only weakens the Christian debater's credibility.

judaism.title: Judaism
judaism.lead: A note before this section: one commonly circulated claim — that the Talmud permits or condones violence against, or denies the humanity of, non-Jews — is not found in the actual Talmudic text. It is a well-documented antisemitic fabrication with a long history of being used to incite violence against Jewish communities, built on invented or deliberately mistranslated 'quotations.' It is not included here because there is no accurate, sourced version of it to present; treating a hate-propaganda claim as a legitimate debate question would misinform readers regardless of framing. What follows instead are the real, substantive theological questions in Jewish-Christian dialogue, including a genuine and fair question about the Talmud's actual role and authority.

hinduism.title: Hinduism
hinduism.lead: Hinduism is not a single unified system but a family of related traditions (Vedanta, Vaishnavism, Shaivism, Shaktism, and many regional and philosophical schools) spanning strict monism, qualified dualism, and personal theism. The questions below try to respect that internal diversity rather than treating 'Hinduism' as one monolithic doctrine — a mistake that undermines credibility as quickly in this context as it does with Islam or Judaism.

sikhism.title: Sikhism
sikhism.lead: Sikhism is a distinct, monotheistic tradition founded by Guru Nanak (1469-1539) in the Punjab region, historically in dialogue with both Hindu and Muslim thought of its time but developing its own scripture, theology, and institutions. It should not be treated as a sect of either Hinduism or Islam in comparative apologetics.

questions.title: Does the Qur'an describe Allah as having literal hands, and how is this reconciled with Islamic teaching that Allah is beyond physical form?

blocks.heading: Context
items: The Qur'an repeatedly attributes a 'hand' or 'hands' (yad/yadayn) to Allah, alongside references to His 'face' and sitting on a 'throne' (istawa). Islamic theology insists Allah is utterly transcendent and unlike creation (tanzih), creating a long-running internal debate over how to read these terms.

blocks.heading: Mainstream Position & Primary Sources
items: Ash'ari and Maturidi theologians (the majority Sunni schools) read these as metaphorical expressions of power, favor, or majesty — not literal anatomy.
Traditionalist/Athari and many Salafi scholars (following Ibn Taymiyyah) affirm the terms as real attributes 'without asking how' (bila kayf) and without comparison to created hands.
Both camps agree Allah does not have a body like a human — the disagreement is over whether 'hand' is literal-but-incomparable or purely figurative.

blocks.heading: Primary Source References
items: Qur'an 38:75 — Allah says He created Adam 'with My two hands.'
Qur'an 5:64 — 'the Jews say, Allah's hand is chained... rather His hands are outstretched.'
Qur'an 48:10 — 'the Hand of Allah is over their hands.'

blocks.heading: Christian Apologetic Response
items: Christianity faces a structurally similar question and answers it through the Incarnation: God the Son took on a literal human body (John 1:14), so anthropomorphic language about God is not a problem to be explained away but is fulfilled in Christ.

A fair Christian question to raise is not 'gotcha, your God has hands,' but: if Islam insists Allah cannot truly be seen, touched, or embodied without compromising His transcendence, does that make it harder or easier for God to be genuinely knowable and relational, compared to a God who enters creation in the Incarnation?

blocks.heading: Points for Respectful Discussion
items: This is best raised as a comparative question about how each religion resolves transcendence-versus-relationship, not as a claim that Islamic theology is incoherent — informed Muslims will point out the Ash'ari/Athari debate is centuries old and internally resolved to their own satisfaction.

blocks.heading: Further Resources
items: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy — Islamic Theology

questions.title: How many wives did Muhammad have, and how is this reconciled with the Qur'an's own limit of four wives for Muslim men?

blocks.heading: Context
items: Sources typically count 11 to 13 wives (numbers vary by how betrothals, deaths, and disputed marriages are counted), while Qur'an 4:3 caps ordinary Muslims at four.

blocks.heading: Mainstream Position & Primary Sources
items: Islamic scholarship holds that Qur'an 33:50 grants Muhammad a specific exemption ('a privilege for you only, not for the believers') as part of his unique prophetic role.

Traditional biographical sources (sira) explain the marriages variously as political alliance-building, care for widows of fallen companions, and, in Aisha's case, marriage into Abu Bakr's household to cement the succession relationship.
The marriage to Aisha is itself a genuine point of historical and ethical debate, including among some contemporary Muslim scholars, over the age at which it was contracted versus consummated.

blocks.heading: Primary Source References
items: Qur'an 4:3 — general limit of four wives.
Qur'an 33:50 — exemption granted to Muhammad specifically.
Sahih al-Bukhari 5133 and 3894 — narrations from Aisha regarding her age at marriage and consummation.
Ibn Sa'd, Kitab al-Tabaqat al-Kabir, vol. 8 — biographical listing of Muhammad's wives.

blocks.heading: Christian Apologetic Response
items: Rather than simple mockery of the number, the strongest apologetic angle is a consistency question: does a prophet claiming to deliver universal moral law get to receive a personal exemption from that law, and if so, on what principled basis is that different from any other lawgiver exempting himself?

This can be paired with 1 Timothy 3:2's requirement that a Christian overseer be 'the husband of one wife' as a point of contrast in leadership ethics, without needing exaggerated claims about the exact count.

blocks.heading: Points for Respectful Discussion
items: State the range (11–13) rather than a single number, and acknowledge upfront that Muslims themselves distinguish this as a Muhammad-specific exemption — asserting it as a simple contradiction will be immediately corrected and will cost credibility.

questions.title: Why do some Muslims (particularly in Sufi and Shi'a practice) invoke Ali or other figures for help, and what does mainstream Sunni theology say about this?

blocks.heading: Context
items: Phrases like 'Ya Ali madad' (O Ali, help) are used in some Sufi and Shi'a devotional contexts. This is actually a live internal Islamic controversy, not primarily a Christian-vs-Muslim one.

blocks.heading: Mainstream Position & Primary Sources
items: Mainstream Sunni orthodoxy (including Salafi and most traditional schools) considers calling on any created being — including Ali, saints, or Muhammad himself — for direct help (istighatha) to be a serious theological error, sometimes labeled shirk (associating partners with Allah).
Sufi defenders of the practice argue it is tawassul (seeking intercession through a beloved figure), not worship of that figure, and distinguish it carefully from prayer directed at the person.
Shi'a theology holds Ali and the Imams occupy a unique spiritual station (wilayah) that justifies seeking their intercession, a position rejected by Sunni orthodoxy.

blocks.heading: Primary Source References
items: Qur'an 39:3 — warning against taking intercessors besides Allah.
Qur'an 72:18 — 'the masjids are for Allah, so do not invoke anyone with Allah.'
Ibn Taymiyyah, Majmu' al-Fatawa, vol. 1 — classical critique of grave-veneration and saint invocation.

blocks.heading: Christian Apologetic Response
items: This is most useful as a mirror question: Muhammad himself is held by orthodox Sunni Islam to have no power to help beyond his death, yet millions of Muslims practice tawassul or Sufi devotion to Ali anyway — which raises the question of whether official theology fully controls popular practice in any religion, Christianity included (e.g., debates over the intercession of saints and Mary in Catholic and Orthodox tradition).

Framed this way it becomes a genuinely interesting comparative-religion conversation rather than an attack, since Christians have their own internal Protestant/Catholic/Orthodox debate over intercession.

blocks.heading: Points for Respectful Discussion
items: This question lands better as 'help me understand how Sunni and Shi'a/Sufi Muslims differ on this' than as 'is Muhammad weaker than Ali,' which is not a claim any mainstream Muslim actually makes.

blocks.heading: Further Resources
items: Oxford Islamic Studies — Tawassul and Intercession

questions.title: When and how did Muhammad die, according to the earliest Islamic sources?

blocks.heading: Context
items: Muhammad died in 632 CE in Medina, in the house of his wife Aisha, after an illness of about two weeks.

blocks.heading: Mainstream Position & Primary Sources
items: Islamic tradition holds he died of a fever accompanied by severe headache, with his head resting in Aisha's lap, and was buried where he died.
The illness is described in hadith as beginning after visiting the graveyard of Baqi', with Muhammad reportedly saying Allah gave him a choice between this world and the next.

blocks.heading: Primary Source References
items: Sahih al-Bukhari 4446, 4442, 5666 — accounts of the Prophet's final illness.
Sahih al-Bukhari 198 — burial location in Aisha's house.
Ibn Ishaq, Sirat Rasul Allah (as preserved by Ibn Hisham) — narrative account of the final illness.

blocks.heading: Christian Apologetic Response
items: The comparative value here is contrasting Muhammad's death (natural illness, body remains entombed in Medina) with the Christian claim of Jesus's bodily resurrection and empty tomb — a genuine and central point of theological difference worth exploring on its historical merits.

blocks.heading: Points for Respectful Discussion
items: This is factual ground both traditions largely agree on; the apologetic weight is in what each founder's death is claimed to mean, not in disputing the facts of Muhammad's death itself.

questions.title: Is there a hadith basis for the claim that Muhammad was poisoned, and do Muslim scholars connect this to his death?

blocks.heading: Context
items: This refers to the Khaybar incident, where a Jewish woman named Zaynab bint al-Harith reportedly served Muhammad poisoned meat.

blocks.heading: Mainstream Position & Primary Sources
items: The incident is reported in hadith as occurring years before Muhammad's death, at Khaybar, not administered by Aisha.

Some hadith narrations have Muhammad stating near his death that he still felt the effect of that poison 'cutting his aorta,' which a minority of classical and modern commentators cite as a contributing factor to his final illness; this is not the mainstream causal account, which attributes his death to the fever illness described above.

blocks.heading: Primary Source References
items: Sahih al-Bukhari 4249 — the Khaybar poisoning account.
Sunan Abi Dawud 4512 — Muhammad's later statement connecting the poison to his final illness.

blocks.heading: Christian Apologetic Response
items: The claim that 'Aisha poisoned Muhammad' does not appear in the classical hadith corpus and should not be asserted as fact — using it would be an inaccurate claim that a well-informed Muslim debater would correctly refute, damaging credibility. The verifiable and more interesting point is the Khaybar poisoning itself and Muhammad's own reported uncertainty about his prognosis, which can be contrasted with Gospel accounts of Jesus predicting His own death and resurrection in advance (Mark 8:31).

blocks.heading: Points for Respectful Discussion
items: Stick to what the hadith actually say (Khaybar, years earlier) rather than the popularized 'Aisha poisoned him' claim, which has no solid textual basis.

questions.title: Were Muhammad's parents Muslim, and what does Islamic theology say about the eternal status of those who died before Islam?

blocks.heading: Context
items: Muhammad's father Abdullah died before his birth, and his mother Aminah died when he was about six, both prior to his prophethood in 610 CE.

blocks.heading: Mainstream Position & Primary Sources
items: Mainstream Islamic scholarship classifies them as having lived and died prior to Islam and therefore not Muslims in the technical sense, since the religion had not yet been revealed.

A well-known hadith records Muhammad asking Allah's permission to seek forgiveness for his mother and being refused, then being permitted only to visit her grave — a passage scholars have debated extensively regarding the fate of those who die without receiving the message (ahl al-fatra).

blocks.heading: Primary Source References
items: Sahih Muslim 976 — Muhammad's request to seek forgiveness for his mother refused; permission to visit her grave granted.
Qur'an 17:15 — 'We do not punish until We have sent a messenger' — cited in the ahl al-fatra debate.

blocks.heading: Christian Apologetic Response
items: This opens a genuine comparative theology conversation about the fate of the unevangelized — Islam and Christianity both wrestle with this question (compare Romans 2:12-16), and it's a substantive area for dialogue rather than a rhetorical trap.

blocks.heading: Points for Respectful Discussion
items: Present as a real, debated question within Islamic scholarship (there are multiple schools of thought on ahl al-fatra), not as a 'gotcha' about Muhammad's own family.

blocks.heading: Further Resources
items: Sahih Muslim, Book of Funerals — Sunnah.com

questions.title: Why do pilgrims kiss or touch the Black Stone (Hajar al-Aswad) during Hajj, and is this idol veneration?

blocks.heading: Context
items: The Black Stone is set into a corner of the Ka'aba, and pilgrims traditionally attempt to kiss or touch it during tawaf (circumambulation).

blocks.heading: Mainstream Position & Primary Sources
items: Islamic scholarship is explicit that the stone itself has no divine or independent power, and the act imitates Muhammad's own practice rather than constituting worship of the object.
The caliph Umar ibn al-Khattab is recorded explicitly denying any inherent power in the stone and framing the kiss purely as following the Prophet's example.

blocks.heading: Primary Source References
items: Sahih al-Bukhari 1597 — Umar's statement: 'I know that you are a stone that neither benefits nor harms; had I not seen the Prophet kiss you, I would not have kissed you.'

blocks.heading: Christian Apologetic Response
items: Because mainstream Islamic scholars themselves already reject any claim that this is idol worship, framing it that way to a Muslim audience is inaccurate and easily deflected. The more productive comparative question is about the role of physical ritual and sacred objects in worship generally — Christianity has its own history of debate over relics, icons, and physical veneration (the iconoclasm controversies), so this works better as a shared reflection than an accusation.

blocks.heading: Points for Respectful Discussion
items: Avoid the 'idol worship' framing entirely in debate — it is factually contested by the tradition's own core texts and will not land as intended.

blocks.heading: Further Resources
items: Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of Hajj — Sunnah.com

questions.title: What do the Qur'an and hadith actually teach about jihad, and how does this map onto modern conflicts (e.g., discussions around Israel–Palestine)?

blocks.heading: Context
items: Jihad is a broad Arabic term meaning 'struggle,' encompassing personal spiritual effort, non-violent striving, and armed conflict under specific conditions. It is one of the most contested terms in Muslim-non-Muslim dialogue precisely because of this range.

blocks.heading: Mainstream Position & Primary Sources
items: Classical jurisprudence (fiqh al-jihad) distinguishes defensive jihad (obligatory on all when a Muslim land is attacked) from offensive jihad (historically debated, requiring authorization by a legitimate ruler/caliph, largely inapplicable in the absence of a caliphate today according to most mainstream scholars).

The widely circulated hadith calling armed combat the 'lesser jihad' versus the 'greater jihad' of struggling against one's own sin is graded by most hadith scholars (including al-Bayhaqi and al-Iraqi) as weak (da'if) or without a reliable chain, though it is popular in devotional and Sufi contexts.

The overwhelming majority of contemporary Muslim scholarly bodies (e.g., Al-Azhar) explicitly reject terrorism and the targeting of civilians as violations of Islamic law regarding warfare (which historically prohibited killing non-combatants, per Abu Bakr's instructions to his armies).

blocks.heading: Primary Source References
items: Qur'an 2:190 — 'Fight in the way of Allah those who fight you, but do not transgress; Allah does not love transgressors.'

Qur'an 9:5 (the so-called 'sword verse') and Qur'an 9:29 — often cited in isolation by critics; classical exegesis (tafsir) situates both within a specific historical treaty-violation context (see Ibn Kathir's commentary).
Sunan al-Tirmidhi (hadith on Abu Bakr's instructions against killing non-combatants, destroying property, or harming monks).

blocks.heading: Christian Apologetic Response
items: A fair apologetic approach acknowledges the internal diversity above rather than treating 'jihad' as a single monolithic doctrine, then raises the substantive question: unlike the New Testament, which contains no divine sanction for Christians to wage religious war (contrast with Matthew 26:52, 'those who live by the sword will die by the sword'), the Qur'an and hadith do contain specific verses regulating armed conflict for religious ends — what does that mean for how the religion's founding texts, as opposed to any individual believer's actions, relate to violence?

This is a real point of theological contrast worth exploring, but it should be raised as a textual-comparison question, not as an accusation about what 'Muslims want,' since surveys and mainstream Muslim scholarship consistently show most Muslims do not support such violence.

blocks.heading: Points for Respectful Discussion
items: This is the single most sensitive topic in the chapter. Framing it as a slur against ordinary Muslims ('why do Muslims love jihad') is both inaccurate and will shut down dialogue immediately. Framing it as an honest textual and historical question about how Islamic law has treated warfare is defensible and has a real scholarly literature to draw on.

blocks.heading: Further Resources
items: Ibn Kathir, Tafsir on Surah 9 (Quran.com commentary)

questions.title: Do early Islamic sources record Muhammad's companions fleeing during battle?

blocks.heading: Context
items: Yes — this is explicitly stated in the Qur'an itself regarding the Battle of Uhud and the Battle of Hunayn, and is not a contested historical claim.

blocks.heading: Mainstream Position & Primary Sources
items: The Qur'an describes Muslim forces breaking ranks and fleeing at Uhud after initially winning, due to disobeying orders to hold a defensive position, and again briefly at Hunayn before regrouping.

blocks.heading: Primary Source References
items: Qur'an 3:153 — 'when you climbed [the hill] without looking back at anyone while the Messenger was calling you.'
Qur'an 3:155 — those who fled were 'made to slip by Satan for some of what they earned,' but Allah forgave them.
Qur'an 9:25 — at Hunayn, 'the earth, as vast as it is, was straitened for you, and you turned back in flight.'

blocks.heading: Christian Apologetic Response
items: This is well-documented in the text itself and openly discussed by Muslim commentators as a lesson about obedience and human weakness rather than something requiring concealment. It's most useful in dialogue as evidence that the Qur'an does not present the earliest Muslim community as flawless — a point that can open a broader conversation about how each religion's scripture handles the moral failures of its central figures (compare Peter's denial of Christ, Matthew 26:69-75).

blocks.heading: Points for Respectful Discussion
items: This one requires no reframing — it's a straightforward textual fact already acknowledged in Islamic exegesis, so it's a strong, low-risk factual anchor for a broader conversation about scripture and human fallibility.

questions.title: How do Islamic sources justify military expansion in the early conquests, and how does this relate to modern political conflicts?

blocks.heading: Context
items: Within decades of Muhammad's death, Islamic rule expanded rapidly across the Middle East, North Africa, and beyond through military conquest — a well-documented historical fact, distinct from the theological question of jihad's conditions discussed above.

blocks.heading: Mainstream Position & Primary Sources
items: Classical Islamic historiography (e.g., al-Tabari) presents the early conquests as a mix of religious mission, political consolidation after the Ridda wars, and the expansionist dynamics common to empires of the era.

Contemporary Muslim scholars overwhelmingly distinguish this seventh-century historical and political context from modern nation-state conflicts such as Israel–Palestine, which most religious authorities on both sides frame primarily in nationalist and territorial rather than purely theological terms, whatever religious rhetoric individual actors may add.

blocks.heading: Primary Source References
items: Al-Tabari, Ta'rikh al-Rusul wa'l-Muluk (History of the Prophets and Kings) — primary historiographical source on the early conquests.

blocks.heading: Christian Apologetic Response
items: It is historically inaccurate and unhelpful in dialogue to collapse a modern geopolitical conflict directly into a seventh-century religious question, or vice versa — both sides of that comparison have Muslim, Christian, and secular voices making the same collapsing move for rhetorical convenience. A more honest apologetic contribution is to note that Christianity's own historical entanglement with empire (e.g., the Crusades, colonial-era missions) means this is not a comparison Christians can make from a position of moral high ground, and it's more productive to keep historical and modern political questions analytically separate.

blocks.heading: Points for Respectful Discussion
items: This question is easily misused to make current political conflicts a referendum on Islam's truth-claims; resist that move on both historical and charitable grounds.

blocks.heading: Further Resources
items: Al-Tabari's History (translated volumes, SUNY Press index)

questions.title: Does Islam prescribe the death penalty for apostasy (ridda), and how is this reconciled with 'no compulsion in religion'?

blocks.heading: Context
items: Classical Islamic law (fiqh) across the major Sunni schools prescribes capital punishment for an adult Muslim who openly leaves Islam, while the Qur'an itself never states an earthly death penalty for apostasy and contains verses affirming freedom of belief — a tension debated intensely within Islam today.

blocks.heading: Mainstream Position & Primary Sources
items: The death penalty rests primarily on hadith: 'Whoever changes his religion, kill him' (Sahih al-Bukhari 6922), plus reports of Muhammad's companions executing apostates (Sahih Muslim 1676). All four Sunni madhhabs historically affirmed it, with procedural differences — e.g., a waiting period (istitaba) to invite repentance, and the Hanafi school prescribing imprisonment rather than execution for female apostates.

Many modern Muslim scholars and apologists argue the hadith targeted political treason and rebellion (hirabah) in a nascent state rather than private change of belief, citing Qur'an 2:256 ('no compulsion in religion'), 4:137 (which describes people believing then disbelieving with no earthly penalty mentioned), and 18:29 ('let whoever wills believe, and whoever wills disbelieve').

In practice, enforcement varies enormously: a minority of states criminalize apostasy capitally today, while most Muslim-majority countries do not enforce it, and many prominent contemporary scholars (e.g., figures associated with Al-Azhar reform currents, and scholars such as Abdullah Saeed) argue for full freedom of religion.

blocks.heading: Primary Source References
items: Sahih al-Bukhari 6922 — 'Whoever changes his religion, kill him.'
Sahih Muslim 1676 — execution of apostates among Muhammad's companions.
Qur'an 2:256 — 'There is no compulsion in religion.'
Qur'an 4:137; 18:29 — passages cited against a Qur'anic death penalty.

blocks.heading: Christian Apologetic Response
items: The strongest fair version of this question presses the internal tension rather than caricaturing Muslims: if the Qur'an affirms no compulsion, on what principled basis does a later hadith-based penalty override it, and does that penalty effectively coerce conscience?

Contrast with the New Testament pattern: when disciples abandoned Jesus over hard teaching, He let them go and asked the Twelve whether they too would leave (John 6:66-67) — persuasion without coercion — and the apostolic church is given no command to punish leavers with death (compare 2 Timothy 2:24-25).

blocks.heading: Points for Respectful Discussion
items: Distinguish classical jurisprudence from the views and practice of individual Muslims — many Muslims today oppose the death penalty for apostasy, and attributing support for it to every Muslim is inaccurate and will shut down dialogue. Frame it as a question about texts and legal history.

blocks.heading: Further Resources
items: Abdullah Saeed on freedom of religion (academic overview)

questions.title: What do the Qur'an and hadith teach about slavery — do they abolish it, regulate it, or permit its continuation?

blocks.heading: Context
items: The Qur'an and hadith presuppose the existence of slavery (riqq), regulate its practice, strongly encourage manumission as a meritorious act, but never command its abolition — a factual description mainstream Muslim scholarship accepts while debating its implications.

blocks.heading: Mainstream Position & Primary Sources
items: Classical fiqh codified lawful enslavement (primarily captives of lawful war), the mukataba contract by which a slave could buy freedom (Qur'an 24:33), expiation of sins through freeing slaves (Qur'an 4:92, 5:89, 90:13), and detailed rules on treatment — while continuing to permit the institution itself.

Contemporary mainstream scholars overwhelmingly hold slavery to be abolished and impermissible today, arguing either that the Qur'an's ethic of emancipation pointed toward gradual abolition (a view associated with modernists such as Fazlur Rahman and many Azhari scholars), or that international consensus (ijma) and public interest (maslaha) have closed a door the texts left open in the seventh century. A small literalist fringe has at times (e.g., ISIS propaganda, 2014-2019) claimed revival is permissible — a position condemned by virtually all recognized scholarly bodies.

Abolition in Muslim-majority lands came historically through colonial-era and modern state law (e.g., Ottoman firman of 1857 restricting the trade, Saudi abolition in 1962, Mauritania's repeated abolitions culminating in 2007 criminalization), not through a classical consensus that the texts themselves abolished it.

blocks.heading: Primary Source References
items: Qur'an 90:12-13; 4:92; 5:89 — freeing slaves as righteousness and expiation.
Sahih al-Bukhari 6715; Sahih Muslim 1657 — hadith on treatment and manumission.

blocks.heading: Christian Apologetic Response
items: The fair apologetic question is about the nature of a claimed final, universal moral law: if the Qur'an is the complete and final moral legislation for all times, why does it regulate but never abolish slavery, while the New Testament — though written into a slaveholding world — plants the theological seeds (Philemon, Galatians 3:28, 1 Timothy 1:10 listing slave-traders among the lawless) that the church eventually used to abolish it?

This must be raised with humility: Christians defended chattel slavery from the Bible for centuries, and the abolitionist victory was won by Christians arguing against other Christians. The honest framing is textual and trajectory-based, not a claim of a clean Christian record.

blocks.heading: Points for Respectful Discussion
items: Acknowledge upfront that mainstream Muslim scholarship today rejects slavery and condemned ISIS-style revival claims — the question is about what the founding texts say and how abolition is theologically grounded, not an accusation about what ordinary Muslims believe.

blocks.heading: Further Resources
items: Encyclopaedia of the Qur'an — 'Slaves and Slavery'
Al-Azhar statements condemning ISIS revival of slavery (Al-Azhar Observatory)

questions.title: What does the phrase 'what your right hands possess' (ma malakat aymanukum) permit, and what do Islamic sources say about concubinage?

blocks.heading: Context
items: The Qur'an permits sexual relations with wives 'or what your right hands possess' — understood unanimously in classical exegesis as female slaves or captives — a permission mainstream scholarship acknowledges while debating its applicability today.

blocks.heading: Mainstream Position & Primary Sources
items: Classical tafsir and fiqh (all four Sunni schools) read Qur'an 4:3, 4:24, 23:5-6 and 33:50 as permitting a male owner sexual access to his female slaves without a marriage contract, alongside detailed regulation (waiting period/istibra after capture, prohibition on selling a concubine who bears her master's child — umm al-walad — per Umar's ruling, etc.). Hadith literature discusses the practice openly, including coitus interruptus (azl) with captives (Sahih Muslim 1438).

Modern scholars divide: the mainstream position holds the rulings are inoperative today because lawful slavery no longer exists (hence the permission has no present object), while a minority of traditionalists hold the text's permission remains in principle if lawful captivity ever recurred. Virtually all recognized authorities condemn any modern revival (e.g., ISIS's 2014 justifications) as grotesque and unlawful.

The Qur'an simultaneously commands kind treatment of captives in some passages (76:8) and — in the same breath as the permission verses — frames chastity and marriage as the ideal (4:25 encourages marrying believing slave women rather than using them casually).

blocks.heading: Primary Source References
items: Sahih Muslim 1438 — hadith on azl with captives.
Qur'an 4:25; 76:8 — marriage preference and kind treatment passages.

blocks.heading: Christian Apologetic Response
items: The substantive contrast is with the New Testament sexual ethic, which permits sexual relations only within marriage, requires mutual consent and dignity within it (1 Corinthians 7:3-4, 1 Thessalonians 4:3-6, Hebrews 13:4), and never creates a category of persons sexually available outside marriage by virtue of captivity.

Raised carefully, the question is whether a universal moral code can simultaneously uphold chastity as ideal and permit non-marital sexual access conditioned on war captivity — and, if the answer is 'that was a seventh-century concession,' what principle distinguishes concession from enduring command elsewhere in the same text?

blocks.heading: Points for Respectful Discussion
items: This is among the most sensitive topics in the book. Present the classical position accurately (it is unanimously attested, so denying it exists destroys credibility), acknowledge the mainstream modern inoperability argument fairly, and never weaponize it as a slur against individual Muslims — engage the texts and the interpretive reasoning.

questions.title: Who physically wrote down the Qur'an's verses, and what was his relationship to Muhammad?

blocks.heading: Context
items: The Qur'an's content is held by Islamic belief to have been revealed to Muhammad orally through the angel Jibril; Muhammad himself dictated it to scribes.

blocks.heading: Mainstream Position & Primary Sources
items: The principal scribe named in tradition is Zayd ibn Thabit, a companion of Muhammad from Medina (not a blood relative), who later led the Qur'an's compilation under Abu Bakr and its standardization under Uthman.
Other companions also served as scribes at various points, including Ali ibn Abi Talib (Muhammad's cousin and son-in-law), Ubayy ibn Ka'b, and Uthman ibn Affan himself.

blocks.heading: Primary Source References
items: Sahih al-Bukhari 4986 — Zayd ibn Thabit's account of being commissioned to collect the Qur'an.
Sahih al-Bukhari 4987 — Zayd ibn Thabit's role in the Uthmanic standardization.

blocks.heading: Christian Apologetic Response
items: This is well-attested and not seriously disputed; it's most useful as a bridge into the compilation-history question (Q14 below) rather than as a standalone point.

blocks.heading: Points for Respectful Discussion
items: Straightforward factual question with a clear, sourced answer — good as background before raising the more substantive compilation debate.

blocks.heading: Further Resources
items: Sahih al-Bukhari, Virtues of the Qur'an — Sunnah.com

questions.title: Was Muhammad literate, and what does the Qur'an's description of him as 'ummi' mean?

blocks.heading: Context
items: Islamic tradition has generally held Muhammad could not read or write, taking this as evidence that the Qur'an's literary sophistication could not be his own composition — an argument for its divine origin (i'jaz al-Qur'an).

blocks.heading: Mainstream Position & Primary Sources
items: The standard reading of 'al-nabi al-ummi' (Qur'an 7:157-158) is 'the unlettered/illiterate prophet,' supporting the traditional doctrine.

A minority of scholars, both classical and modern, argue 'ummi' more precisely means 'belonging to a people without a prior scripture' (i.e., a gentile relative to the Jewish and Christian scriptural traditions) rather than strictly 'illiterate,' noting Muhammad's mercantile background involved trade and contracts.

blocks.heading: Primary Source References
items: Qur'an 29:48 — 'you did not recite before it any scripture, nor did you inscribe one with your right hand' — cited in support of the illiteracy reading.

blocks.heading: Christian Apologetic Response
items: This is a genuinely open internal debate rather than a settled contradiction, so the strongest apologetic use of it is simply presenting the ambiguity itself as a case study — alongside the Bible's own claims about its human authors writing under divine inspiration (2 Timothy 3:16, 2 Peter 1:21) — in how each religion grounds a claim to supernatural textual origin.

blocks.heading: Points for Respectful Discussion
items: Present both readings; asserting Muhammad was 'definitely literate' as a gotcha overstates the historical certainty and will be met with a legitimate scholarly rebuttal.

questions.title: Is there a hadith describing Qur'anic verses being lost, including a report about a domestic animal eating a written page?

blocks.heading: Context
items: Yes — this is a real, authenticated hadith from Aisha, frequently raised in Christian-Muslim textual debates, and deserves accurate presentation.

blocks.heading: Mainstream Position & Primary Sources
items: Aisha reported that a verse on stoning (rajm) was written on a page kept under her pillow, and that after Muhammad's death, a 'tame animal' entered and ate it while the household was occupied with his funeral.

Mainstream Islamic scholarship's response is that the Qur'an's preservation rests primarily on parallel, simultaneous oral memorization by many companions (huffaz), not solely on written pages, so the loss of one physical page does not, in this view, compromise the integrity of the memorized and later-compiled text; some scholars also treat this narration as referring to a verse whose recitation (but not legal ruling) was later abrogated.

blocks.heading: Primary Source References
items: Sunan Ibn Majah 1944 — Aisha's report on the stoning verse and the animal.
Musnad Ahmad ibn Hanbal 25889 — parallel narration.

blocks.heading: Christian Apologetic Response
items: This is one of the more substantive textual-critical questions in the chapter and should be presented accurately rather than sensationalized ('goat ate the Qur'an' framings overstate and simplify a real hadith). The productive comparative angle is putting Islamic and Christian textual transmission side by side: Islam relies on a claim of parallel oral and written preservation from the start, while the New Testament's reliability rests on an early and extensive manuscript tradition — both are legitimate grounds for a textual-criticism conversation, and both traditions have their own internal literature defending their transmission.

blocks.heading: Points for Respectful Discussion
items: Cite the actual hadith (Ibn Majah 1944) rather than a paraphrased internet version, and expect a well-prepared Muslim respondent to raise the oral-preservation and abrogation responses — engage with those directly rather than repeating the question.

questions.title: Why were Abu Bakr's and Uthman's compilations of the Qur'an necessary if the text was already what Allah sent down?

blocks.heading: Context
items: This is arguably the strongest and most substantive question in the chapter, and it parallels the kind of textual-criticism questions often raised about the Bible — so it deserves to be handled with particular care and consistency.

blocks.heading: Mainstream Position & Primary Sources
items: Tradition holds the Qur'an was preserved during Muhammad's life through both memorization and scattered written fragments (on parchment, bone, palm leaves), but was not bound into a single codex.

After the Battle of Yamama (633 CE) killed a significant number of huffaz, Abu Bakr commissioned Zayd ibn Thabit to gather the fragments and memorized material into a single master copy, primarily as a preservation measure.

By the time of Uthman (roughly 650-656 CE), regional variations in recitation had caused disputes between Muslim armies from different provinces; Uthman commissioned a standardized master copy (the 'Uthmanic codex') and ordered other regional copies and variant readings destroyed to enforce a single textual standard, while still preserving several accepted oral qira'at (recitation styles) within that standardized consonantal skeleton.

blocks.heading: Primary Source References
items: Sahih al-Bukhari 4986 — Abu Bakr's compilation after Yamama.
Sahih al-Bukhari 4987 — Uthman's standardization and the destruction of variant copies.

blocks.heading: Christian Apologetic Response
items: The honest and intellectually consistent apologetic move is to acknowledge that this is a real and legitimate textual-history question for Islam, while also acknowledging that the New Testament has its own, differently-structured textual history (a large body of early manuscripts with minor variants, rather than a single official standardization event that destroyed alternatives) — and to argue on the merits which model provides stronger grounds for confidence in transmission, rather than pretending only one tradition has a textual history to account for.

A double standard to avoid: treating any editorial/compilation process in the Qur'an's history as fatal to its reliability while treating a comparable (in fact more complex) manuscript history for the Bible as unproblematic. Consistency here is what makes the apologetic credible.

blocks.heading: Points for Respectful Discussion
items: This is the strongest and most respected question in serious Christian-Muslim textual debate (raised seriously by scholars like Jay Smith); it should be argued on textual-criticism merits, and a Christian debater should be equally ready to answer the parallel question about the Bible's own transmission history.

blocks.heading: Further Resources
items: Sahih al-Bukhari, Virtues of the Qur'an — Sunnah.com
Encyclopaedia of the Qur'an — 'Codices of the Qur'an'

questions.title: What is the doctrine of abrogation (naskh), and does it mean the Qur'an contradicts itself?

blocks.heading: Context
items: The Qur'an itself states that Allah replaces revelations (2:106; 16:101), and classical scholarship developed the doctrine of naskh (abrogation) to systematize verses whose rulings appear to conflict — a mainstream doctrine with a genuinely debated scope.

blocks.heading: Mainstream Position & Primary Sources
items: The majority classical position (e.g., Al-Suyuti in Al-Itqan) affirms naskh both within the Qur'an (later verses replacing earlier rulings, such as the gradual restriction of wine: 2:219 → 4:43 → 5:90) and of earlier scriptures by the Qur'an. Proposed counts of abrogated verses vary wildly — from a handful to several hundred — because scholars disagree on the criteria, a fact critics cite and defenders concede.

A minority, classical (Abu Muslim al-Isfahani) and modern (e.g., Muhammad Abu Zahra, modernists such as Abdullahi an-Na'im's teacher Mahmoud Taha inverts the scheme), deny or radically minimize intra-Qur'anic abrogation, preferring harmonization (takhsis — specification — rather than replacement).

The most debated application concerns the 'sword verse' (9:5), which some classical exegetes (e.g., reports attributed to Ibn Abbas via Ali ibn Abi Talhah) said abrogated dozens of peaceful verses — a wide-scope claim rejected by many other exegetes (including Al-Tabari and modern commentators such as Al-Qaradawi's school), who read 9:5 as context-specific rather than globally abrogating.

blocks.heading: Primary Source References
items: Qur'an 2:106 — 'Whatever verse We abrogate or cause to be forgotten, We bring one better or similar.'
Al-Suyuti, Al-Itqan fi Ulum al-Qur'an — classical systematization of naskh.

blocks.heading: Christian Apologetic Response
items: Two fair questions arise. First, a coherence question: if the Qur'an is the eternal, uncreated speech of Allah (the Ash'ari doctrine of kalam nafsi), what does it mean for eternal speech to contain successive replacements indexed to seventh-century circumstances — and who decides, given the enormous scholarly disagreement over which verses are abrogated?

Second, a comparative one: Christianity handles Old-to-New development through fulfillment (Matthew 5:17 — Christ fulfills rather than deletes), with the earlier text retained as Scripture; Islam's model replaces rulings while retaining both wordings in the mushaf. Which model better preserves textual integrity is a legitimate topic — argued, as always, with acknowledgment that progressive revelation per se is common to both faiths.

blocks.heading: Points for Respectful Discussion
items: Cite the disagreement over scope (handful vs. hundreds) accurately — asserting a single fixed list of abrogated verses will be corrected immediately, since no such consensus list exists. And distinguish abrogation of ruling (hukm) with retention of wording (tilawa) from removal of wording, a distinction the literature carefully maintains.

blocks.heading: Further Resources
items: Al-Suyuti, Al-Itqan (English overview of abrogation chapters)

questions.title: Is Muhammad regarded as fully human, or as a being of divine light (Nur), in Islamic theology?

blocks.heading: Context
items: This is a genuine and long-running internal Sunni debate, most visible in South Asian Islam between the Barelvi and Deobandi/Salafi movements.

blocks.heading: Mainstream Position & Primary Sources
items: The Deobandi and Salafi position, and the plain reading of several Qur'anic verses, holds Muhammad was fully human (bashar) who received revelation, with no ontological difference from other people except prophethood.

The Barelvi position holds Muhammad possessed a unique quality of primordial 'light' (nur), often citing a hadith that 'the first thing Allah created was my light' — a hadith not found in the six canonical (Sunni) collections and graded weak or unreliable by mainstream hadith scholars, though it remains popular in Sufi devotional theology.

blocks.heading: Primary Source References
items: Qur'an 18:110 — 'Say, I am only a man like you, to whom it has been revealed...'

Qur'an 33:45-46 — Muhammad described as 'siraj al-munir' (an illuminating lamp), the verse Barelvi scholars cite as light imagery, though most exegetes read it as a metaphor for guidance, not a claim about his substance.

blocks.heading: Christian Apologetic Response
items: This is a useful comparison point precisely because Christian doctrine has a well-defined, creedal answer to an analogous question — the Logos becoming flesh while remaining fully divine (John 1:1, 1:14) — whereas Islam's own scholars are divided on whether Muhammad is ontologically just a man. Rather than mocking the division, the strongest move is asking a Muslim conversation partner directly which view they hold and why, since it reveals real diversity within Sunni Islam most outsiders assume is monolithic.

blocks.heading: Points for Respectful Discussion
items: Avoid asserting either position as 'the' Islamic view — cite it as an active internal debate, since misstating it as settled will be corrected immediately by an informed Muslim from either camp.

blocks.heading: Further Resources
items: Overview of Barelvi–Deobandi theological differences (Oxford Bibliographies)

questions.title: What does Islam teach about Muhammad's ability to intercede for believers on Judgment Day, and how does this compare to the Christian doctrine of Christ's atonement?

blocks.heading: Context
items: It's inaccurate to say Islam teaches Muhammad has no role at the end times — mainstream Sunni doctrine explicitly affirms a form of prophetic intercession (shafa'ah). The real point of contrast with Christianity is the kind of help offered, not whether any is offered.

blocks.heading: Mainstream Position & Primary Sources
items: Hadith affirm Muhammad will occupy 'al-Maqam al-Mahmud' (the Praiseworthy Station) and will intercede on behalf of believers so that judgment can begin, and separately for grave sinners among his community to be admitted to Paradise.
Crucially, this intercession is granted by Allah's permission and does not remove the requirement that each individual's deeds be weighed — Muhammad does not bear anyone else's sin or guilt.

blocks.heading: Primary Source References
items: Sahih al-Bukhari 4712 and 7510 — hadith on Muhammad's intercession.
Qur'an 53:38 — 'no bearer of burdens will bear the burden of another,' cited by Muslim scholars against any doctrine of substitutionary atonement.

blocks.heading: Christian Apologetic Response
items: This is the real and substantive theological fork: Islamic intercession is advocacy — asking Allah for leniency on behalf of someone whose own deeds are still weighed — while the Christian doctrine of atonement (2 Corinthians 5:21, Isaiah 53:5-6) is substitutionary — Christ actually bearing the penalty for sin so the believer's standing is not based on the weight of their own deeds. That distinction, argued honestly, is a stronger apologetic point than the false claim that Muhammad offers 'no help at all.'

blocks.heading: Points for Respectful Discussion
items: Get the Islamic position right before critiquing it — Qur'an 53:38 is exactly the verse a well-informed Muslim will raise to reject the Christian doctrine of atonement, so be ready to engage it directly.

blocks.heading: Further Resources
items: Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of Tawhid — Sunnah.com

questions.title: Does Islam teach free will or predestination (qadar), and can humans be morally responsible without freedom?

blocks.heading: Context
items: Islam affirms both divine decree and human responsibility without fully resolving their tension — and its internal schools map almost the entire logical space, from near-determinism to libertarian freedom.

blocks.heading: Mainstream Position & Primary Sources
items: The Qur'an contains both registers: comprehensive decree passages (54:49 — 'We created all things in due measure'; 76:29-30 — 'you do not will except that Allah wills') and responsibility passages (18:29 — 'let whoever wills believe'; 41:46 — 'whoever does righteousness, it is for his soul'). Hadith sharpen the decree side: the pen writing all destinies before creation and the embryo's fate (livelihood, lifespan, misery/happiness) written in the womb (Sahih Muslim 2643-2647; Sahih al-Bukhari 6594).

Classical schools divide: the Jabriyya (and popular fatalism) leaned determinist; the Mu'tazila and (differently) Shi'a theologians affirmed strong human freedom to preserve divine justice (adl); Sunni orthodoxy settled between them — Ash'aris via kasb ('acquisition': Allah creates the act, the human 'acquires' it and is responsible), Maturidis granting humans more genuine efficacy (ikhtiyar). Most ordinary Sunnis live somewhere in this middle without technical precision.
One of the six articles of Sunni faith (iman) is belief in qadar — divine decree, good and evil — making this non-optional doctrine, not peripheral speculation.

blocks.heading: Primary Source References
items: Qur'an 54:49; 76:29-30 — decree passages; Qur'an 18:29; 41:46 — responsibility passages.
Sahih Muslim 2643-2647; Sahih al-Bukhari 6594 — the pen and the embryo hadith.
Al-Ash'ari, Al-Ibanah; Al-Maturidi, Kitab al-Tawhid — classical formulations of kasb vs. human efficacy.

blocks.heading: Christian Apologetic Response
items: Christianity has its own unresolved version of this debate (Augustinian/Calvinist sovereignty vs. Arminian freedom, Romans 9 vs. 1 Timothy 2:4), so this works best as a shared-philosophy conversation rather than a one-sided attack: how does each tradition ground moral responsibility, petitionary prayer, and evangelism if God has decreed all things?

The distinctive Christian question to press gently is about the Ash'ari denial of secondary causation (occasionalism — Allah directly creates every event moment by moment): if even human acts are created by Allah and merely 'acquired,' in what sense is the human the author of the act in a way that justifies eternal reward or punishment? Maturidi and Mu'tazili Muslims will press the same question against Ash'aris — you are joining an internal debate, not inventing one.

blocks.heading: Points for Respectful Discussion
items: Ask which school a conversation partner follows before critiquing — 'Islam teaches fatalism' will be (rightly) rejected by Mu'tazili, Shi'a, and Maturidi interlocutors, and even Ash'aris insist kasb preserves responsibility. Present the spectrum.

blocks.heading: Further Resources
items: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy — Islamic Theology (qadar/kasb sections)

questions.title: Can a Muslim have assurance of salvation, or does entry to Paradise remain uncertain until the scales are weighed?

blocks.heading: Context
items: Mainstream Islam teaches that no one (save those explicitly promised Paradise in the texts) can be certain of their final fate in this life — deeds are weighed on the scales (mizan), and entry to Paradise comes by Allah's mercy, not by earned entitlement.

blocks.heading: Mainstream Position & Primary Sources
items: The Qur'an describes the weighing of deeds (7:8-9; 21:47; 101:6-9): 'those whose scales are heavy' prosper, 'those whose scales are light' lose their souls. Hadith add that no one enters Paradise by deeds alone — 'not even me, unless Allah envelops me in His mercy' (Sahih al-Bukhari 5673; Sahih Muslim 2816). Even Muhammad is reported seeking forgiveness daily (Sahih al-Bukhari 6307).

Exceptions in the tradition: martyrs (shuhada) are promised immediate Paradise (3:169), and the 'ten promised Paradise' (al-ashara al-mubashshara) among the companions — categories some extremist recruiters have exploited, which mainstream scholars condemn as manipulation of texts whose conditions (lawful jihad under legitimate authority) are absent.
Sufi and devotional traditions cultivate hope (raja) balanced with fear (khawf), but classical theology treats presumptuous certainty (amn) about one's own salvation as itself blameworthy.

blocks.heading: Primary Source References
items: Sahih al-Bukhari 5673; Sahih Muslim 2816 — 'none will enter by deeds alone.'
Qur'an 39:53 — 'do not despair of Allah's mercy' — the hope passage.

blocks.heading: Christian Apologetic Response
items: The pastoral contrast is direct: the New Testament offers present-tense assurance grounded in Christ's finished work rather than in the believer's deed-weight — 'I write these things to you who believe in the name of the Son of God so that you may know that you have eternal life' (1 John 5:13; cf. Ephesians 2:8-9, Romans 8:1). The question to pose is pastoral rather than polemical: is it good news that even the most devout cannot know, and what does that uncertainty do to love, worship, and fear?

Frame intercession (Q16) and assurance together: Islamic intercession is advocacy for those whose scales are light; Christian atonement is substitution that renders the scales satisfied in Christ. That is the real fork — argue it directly and sympathetically.

blocks.heading: Points for Respectful Discussion
items: Many Muslims find profound humility and motivation in this uncertainty and hear Christian 'assurance' as presumption — listen to that concern (Christian theology also warns against false assurance, Matthew 7:21-23) before pressing the pastoral cost of never knowing. This question persuades through compassion, not pressure.

blocks.heading: Further Resources
items: Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of Patients/Heart-softening — Sunnah.com

questions.title: Both the Qur'an and the Old Testament contain divine commands related to warfare — how does each tradition explain this, and what does the New Testament say by comparison?

blocks.heading: Context
items: This is a fair, symmetrical question and should be treated as one — a Muslim debater will reasonably raise Old Testament conquest texts (e.g., the herem campaigns against Canaanite cities) the moment a Christian raises Qur'anic warfare verses, so both should be addressed together.

blocks.heading: Mainstream Position & Primary Sources
items: Qur'anic warfare verses (9:5, 47:4, 8:12) are read by classical exegetes within the specific context of treaty violations and active conflict during Muhammad's lifetime, and remain part of the Qur'an's continuing legal text.

Old Testament conquest commands (Deuteronomy 20:16-17, 1 Samuel 15:3) are read by Christian theology as commands specific to a bounded historical moment (the conquest of Canaan under the Mosaic covenant), not as a standing legal code for believers today.

blocks.heading: Primary Source References
items: Deuteronomy 20:16-17; 1 Samuel 15:3 — Old Testament conquest commands.
Matthew 26:52; Romans 12:19-21 — New Testament teaching, given directly by Jesus and the apostles, explicitly renouncing violence for believers.

blocks.heading: Christian Apologetic Response
items: The strongest, most honest version of this argument is not 'my scripture has no violence and yours does' — the Old Testament plainly does. It's that the New Testament — the part of the Bible that actually governs Christian conduct after Christ — contains no comparable command, whereas the Qur'an's warfare verses sit within the same continuously-binding text Muslims draw legal rulings from today. That is a real structural difference worth defending, but only if the Old Testament material is acknowledged honestly rather than ignored.

blocks.heading: Points for Respectful Discussion
items: Do not present this as 'the Bible has no violence' — that claim is false and will be immediately and correctly refuted. The defensible claim is about which portion of each scripture is treated as currently binding.

questions.title: Since the name 'Yahweh' and belief in the God of Israel predates Islam by many centuries, does that give it a stronger claim to being the one true God?

blocks.heading: Context
items: This question needs a factual correction before the theological point can be made honestly: 'Allah' is simply the Arabic word for 'God,' cognate with the Hebrew 'Elohim' and Aramaic 'Alaha,' and was used by Arabic-speaking Jews and Christians before Islam existed — it is not a distinct deity name invented by Muhammad or borrowed from a separate pagan god. A once-popular claim that 'Allah' derives from a pre-Islamic moon deity is considered discredited by mainstream historians and linguists and should not be used, as it will be easily and correctly rebutted.

blocks.heading: Mainstream Position & Primary Sources
items: Muslims hold that Allah is the same Creator God worshipped by Abraham, Moses, and the prophets, and that Islam represents a restoration of that original monotheism rather than a new religion.

blocks.heading: Primary Source References
items: Qur'an 29:46 — 'our God and your God is one.'
Qur'an 2:133 — Abraham, Ishmael, and Isaac's God identified as the same God.

blocks.heading: Christian Apologetic Response
items: The theologically honest version of this question is not about the age or etymology of a name — it's about whether the character and self-revelation of God as described in Islam (strict, undivided unity) and as described in Christianity (Trinitarian, self-giving in the Incarnation) can both be the same God, given they make mutually exclusive claims about His nature. That is a real, substantive disagreement worth having; an argument based on which name is 'older' is not, since both traditions trace their God-language back to the same ancient Semitic root.

blocks.heading: Points for Respectful Discussion
items: Drop the 'older name equals truer God' framing and the moon-god theory entirely — both are historically weak and will cost credibility with an informed audience. Focus the conversation on the actual doctrinal disagreement (Trinity vs. strict monotheism).

blocks.heading: Further Resources
items: Encyclopaedia of the Qur'an — 'God and His Attributes'

questions.title: Does the Qur'an itself contain a warning that Allah would 'cut the aorta' of Muhammad if he lied, and is there a hadith connecting this to his death?

blocks.heading: Context
items: This is a real and interesting argument used by some Christian debaters (as noted in Q5), built on a genuine textual parallel — but it should be stated precisely, since the popular version ('Aisha poisoned him') is not accurate.

blocks.heading: Mainstream Position & Primary Sources
items: Qur'an 69:44-46 states that if Muhammad had invented false sayings and attributed them to Allah, Allah would have seized him by the right hand and 'cut his aorta (wateen).'
Separately, a hadith has Muhammad stating near the end of his life that he still felt the effect of poisoned meat eaten years earlier at Khaybar, describing it as 'cutting my aorta.'

blocks.heading: Primary Source References
items: Sunan Abi Dawud 4512 — Muhammad's statement connecting his final illness to the Khaybar poisoning.

blocks.heading: Christian Apologetic Response
items: Presented accurately, this is a legitimate rhetorical point: a Christian debater can note the striking coincidence of language between the Qur'an's self-imposed oath and the hadith's description of Muhammad's own words near death, and ask a Muslim conversation partner how they understand that connection — without asserting the historically unsupported claim that Aisha administered poison.

blocks.heading: Points for Respectful Discussion
items: This argument only works if stated precisely — conflating it with the false poisoning-by-Aisha claim undermines an otherwise genuinely interesting point.

questions.title: The Qur'an calls Jesus 'a Word from Allah' and 'a Spirit from Him' — does it use comparable language for Muhammad, and what does that difference mean?

blocks.heading: Context
items: This is one of the strongest and most textually grounded apologetic points available to a Christian in dialogue with Islam, precisely because it comes directly from the Qur'an's own description of Jesus, not from an outside claim.

blocks.heading: Mainstream Position & Primary Sources
items: The Qur'an gives Jesus unique titles not applied to any other prophet, including Muhammad: 'his word, which He conveyed to Mary, and a spirit from Him' (kalimatuhu... wa ruhun minhu).

Mainstream Islamic theology carefully limits the meaning of these titles to avoid implying divinity — 'word' is read as referring to Jesus's creation by divine command ('Be,' and he was, 3:47) rather than an eternal divine attribute, and 'spirit from Him' as a spirit created and sent by Allah, not a portion of Allah's own being.

blocks.heading: Primary Source References
items: Qur'an 4:171 — 'the Messiah, Jesus son of Mary, was but a messenger of Allah and His word which He conveyed to Mary and a spirit from Him.'
Qur'an 3:45 — Jesus named 'a word from Him.'

blocks.heading: Christian Apologetic Response
items: The apologetic force here is asking why, if these titles carry no special weight, the Qur'an reserves them for Jesus alone and never applies 'word of Allah' or 'spirit from Allah' to Muhammad. This doesn't prove the Christian doctrine of the Logos (John 1:1), but it is a legitimate textual observation worth raising as a question rather than an assertion — let the Muslim conversation partner explain the distinction in their own words.

blocks.heading: Points for Respectful Discussion
items: This is best asked as an open question ('why these titles, and only for Jesus?') rather than a claim that the Qur'an secretly teaches Jesus's divinity, which it explicitly denies elsewhere (Qur'an 5:72-75) and which a Muslim respondent will correctly point out.

questions.title: Does the Qur'an accurately describe the Christian Trinity — and why does it name Mary as part of it?

blocks.heading: Context
items: The Qur'an's two main 'three' passages (4:171; 5:73) warn against saying 'three,' and a third (5:116) depicts Allah asking Jesus whether he told people to take him and his mother as two gods besides Allah — a description no Christian church recognizes as the Trinity.

blocks.heading: Mainstream Position & Primary Sources
items: Mainstream Muslim exegesis (e.g., Ibn Kathir on 5:116) generally reads the verse as addressing real-world excessive Marian veneration (and possibly the Arabian Collyridian sect reported by Epiphanius, which allegedly offered cakes to Mary) rather than quoting the Nicene Creed — i.e., a critique of worship-practice, not of Trinitarian dogma. Modern Muslim apologists (e.g., Shabir Ally, Yasir Qadhi) typically take this line, arguing the Qur'an condemns shirk in whatever form it takes.

Critics (Christian and secular-historical) respond that a revelation claiming to correct Christian error should state the doctrine correctly before refuting it — the Trinity is Father, Son, and Holy Spirit (Matthew 28:19; Nicene Creed, 325/381 CE, two centuries before Islam) — and that 5:116's 'Jesus + Mary + Allah' triad suggests dependence on fringe Arabian practice or hearsay rather than knowledge of mainstream Christian teaching. The Holy Spirit is never named in the Qur'an's 'three' passages at all.

Qur'an 4:171 says 'do not say Three' without defining the three; 5:73 warns those who say 'Allah is the third of three' — both compatible with critiquing tritheism (three gods), which historic Christianity also rejects (one God in three persons, not three gods).

blocks.heading: Primary Source References
items: Qur'an 5:116 — 'Did you say to the people, Take me and my mother as two gods besides Allah?'
Qur'an 4:171; 5:73 — the 'do not say Three' passages.
Matthew 28:19; Nicene Creed — the actual Trinitarian formula, predating Islam by centuries.

blocks.heading: Christian Apologetic Response
items: The fair apologetic point is precise and limited: the Qur'an never once states the doctrine it condemns in terms any Christian would recognize — Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, one being. Ask a Muslim conversation partner to state the Trinity in Christian terms first (most cannot, which proves the communication problem runs both ways), then show that 5:116's triad matches no creed, council, or catechism in Christian history.

Pair with the positive case: the New Testament's Trinitarian grammar (baptismal formula, benedictions like 2 Corinthians 13:14, the Son sending the Spirit in John 14-16) is not tritheism and not Mariolatry — so Qur'anic refutations of tritheism, however true against tritheism, leave Nicene Christianity untouched. Invite engagement with the actual claim.

blocks.heading: Points for Respectful Discussion
items: Do not frame this as 'Muhammad was ignorant' — frame it as a textual-accuracy question about a specific verse. Many informed Muslims already concede 5:116 addresses devotional excess rather than the creed, which is common ground worth affirming before pressing the follow-up: where, then, does the Qur'an engage the actual Nicene claim at all?

blocks.heading: Further Resources
items: Nicene Creed — historical text and context (Britannica)

questions.title: When the Qur'an denies that Allah 'takes a son,' is it refuting what Christians actually believe about Jesus as Son of God?

blocks.heading: Context
items: The Qur'an's denial of divine sonship is consistently framed in physical and procreative terms — Allah has no consort (sahiba), so how could He have a son (6:101); 'He neither begets nor is born' (112:3) — while historic Christian doctrine explicitly denies physical begetting and affirms eternal, non-biological Sonship.

blocks.heading: Mainstream Position & Primary Sources
items: Key verses: 6:101 ('how can He have a son when He has no companion?'), 19:88-92 (the heavens nearly rupture at the claim the Merciful has taken a son), 112:1-4 (Al-Ikhlas: lam yalid wa lam yulad), 4:171 and 19:35 ('it is not for Allah to take a son'). Classical Arabic distinguishes walad (offspring via begetting) from ibn (son, which can be relational/metaphorical) — and the Qur'an's denials cluster around walad language, i.e., procreation.

Historic Christianity agrees Allah/God has no consort and that divine Sonship is not sexual: the Nicene Creed's 'begotten, not made' (gennethenta ou poiethenta) and 'eternally begotten of the Father' precisely exclude physical generation; 'Son' names an eternal relation within the Godhead (John 1:1-3, 14, 18; Hebrews 1:3), not an event in which God fathers a child.

Muslim respondents typically reply that whatever Christians mean, any 'son' language compromises tawhid and that the Qur'an closes the door categorically — a coherent strict-monotheist position, but one that concedes the debate is over the metaphysics of divine unity, not over the caricature of God taking a wife.

blocks.heading: Primary Source References
items: Qur'an 6:101 — 'How can He have a son when He has no companion?'

blocks.heading: Christian Apologetic Response
items: This is arguably the kindest and strongest Trinity-adjacent question in the chapter, because it grants the Qur'an's premise (God has no consort — Christians heartily agree) and asks only that the Qur'an's refutation meet Christianity's actual claim: an eternal Son, 'begotten not made,' without partner, without beginning, without biology. Refuting physical sonship refutes something no Christian confession teaches.

Use the walad/ibn distinction carefully (it is real Arabic, cited by scholars on both sides including Christian Arabists and Muslim exegetes) — then ask: if 'son' in the Bible (Psalm 2:7; John 3:16's monogenes, 'unique/one-of-a-kind') never meant physical offspring to its Jewish and Christian readers, does 6:101's 'no companion, so no son' logic engage that meaning, or only the biological one?

blocks.heading: Points for Respectful Discussion
items: Avoid claiming the Qur'an 'supports' the Trinity (Q20's Word/Spirit titles raise the question but the Qur'an explicitly denies Sonship elsewhere) — the honest claim is narrower: the denial as stated targets procreative sonship, leaving eternal-relational Sonship unaddressed. Let the Muslim partner either defend the broader reading or engage the Nicene one.

questions.title: The Qur'an describes Jesus raising the dead — does it attribute anything comparable to Muhammad, and what does Islamic theology make of that difference?

blocks.heading: Context
items: A fair and interesting comparative-prophetology question, best handled by presenting the Qur'an's own qualifying language rather than ignoring it.

blocks.heading: Mainstream Position & Primary Sources
items: The Qur'an does affirm Jesus healing the blind and lepers and raising the dead, but consistently qualifies each miracle with 'bi'idhni'llah' (by Allah's permission), attributing the power to Allah acting through Jesus, not to Jesus himself.

Muhammad's central and greatest miracle, in Islamic theology, is the Qur'an itself — its literary inimitability (i'jaz) — rather than physical miracles, though some later hadith and tradition literature attribute additional physical miracles to him (e.g., the splitting of the moon, Qur'an 54:1) not narrated with the same detail as Jesus's miracles.

Islamic theology holds Muhammad is the greater prophet not because of a greater quantity of miracles but because he is believed to be the final and most complete bearer of revealed law (khatam al-nabiyyin, Qur'an 33:40).

blocks.heading: Primary Source References
items: Qur'an 3:49 — Jesus healing and raising the dead, 'bi'idhni'llah.'
Qur'an 54:1 — the splitting of the moon.
Qur'an 33:40 — Muhammad as 'the seal of the prophets.'

blocks.heading: Christian Apologetic Response
items: This is a genuinely strong comparative point for a Christian to raise as a question — not as a settled 'gotcha,' since Islamic theology has a ready answer (finality of law, not miracle count, is what makes a prophet greatest) — but it's worth pressing a Muslim conversation partner on why a religion would rank prophets by legal finality rather than by the scope of what God did through them.

blocks.heading: Points for Respectful Discussion
items: Expect the 'khatam al-nabiyyin' response and be ready to engage it directly rather than repeating the miracle comparison, which Islamic theology has already anticipated.

questions.title: Islam affirms Jesus as a prophet but rejects the New Testament's account of his teaching, death, and resurrection — on what textual basis, and is that a consistent position?

blocks.heading: Context
items: This is the most substantive Christological question in Christian-Muslim dialogue, and it's worth engaging directly rather than reducing to a rhetorical jab.

blocks.heading: Mainstream Position & Primary Sources
items: The Qur'an affirms Jesus's virgin birth, many of his miracles, and his status as Messiah and prophet, but explicitly denies both his divinity and his crucifixion, stating instead that 'it was made to appear so to them' and that Allah raised him to Himself.

The Islamic doctrine of tahrif (textual corruption/alteration) holds that the Torah and Gospel Muslims are commanded to respect in their original form (Qur'an 5:46) have since been altered by their custodians, which is how Islamic theology reconciles affirming Jesus's prophethood while rejecting the New Testament's account of his death, resurrection, and divinity as later corruptions.

blocks.heading: Primary Source References
items: Qur'an 4:157 — denial of the crucifixion ('they did not kill him, nor did they crucify him, but it was made to appear so to them').
Qur'an 5:46 — Jesus given the Gospel (Injil) confirming the Torah.
Qur'an 2:75; 5:13 — verses cited for the tahrif doctrine regarding earlier scriptures.

blocks.heading: Christian Apologetic Response
items: The strongest response here is historical rather than purely theological: the manuscript evidence for the New Testament (thousands of early Greek manuscripts, some within decades of the events, plus extensive patristic quotation) predates Islam by five to six centuries and shows textual stability on exactly the points Islam says were corrupted — divinity, crucifixion, resurrection — which raises a specific, answerable historical question: when, how, and by whom would this corruption have occurred, given the manuscript trail?

It is fair and important to acknowledge Islam is not rejecting Jesus outright — it holds him in very high regard as a major prophet — so the disagreement should be framed precisely as being about the reliability of the New Testament text and the nature of Jesus, not as Islam dismissing him.

blocks.heading: Points for Respectful Discussion
items: This is a genuinely productive line of dialogue if pursued through textual/manuscript history rather than assertion — ask specifically when the alleged corruption is claimed to have happened, since the doctrine of tahrif rarely specifies a mechanism or date.

blocks.heading: Further Resources
items: Comparative manuscript-dating overview (Center for the Study of New Testament Manuscripts)

questions.title: Does the Qur'an draw on earlier Jewish and Christian material, and if so, does it contain distinct content of its own?

blocks.heading: Context
items: This is a legitimate academic field (source and intertextual criticism of the Qur'an), and it should be presented as such — the claim that the Qur'an is 'nothing but battles' is an overstatement that a well-read Muslim will easily correct.

blocks.heading: Mainstream Position & Primary Sources
items: Modern source-critical scholarship has documented real parallels between Qur'anic narratives and earlier Jewish (including some Talmudic and Midrashic) and Christian (including apocryphal, non-canonical) material — for example, the story of Cain learning to bury Abel from a raven (Qur'an 5:31) parallels material in Jewish exegetical tradition (Pirke De-Rabbi Eliezer), and Jesus animating clay birds (Qur'an 3:49) closely parallels the non-canonical Infancy Gospel of Thomas.

The Qur'an also contains substantial content not paralleled in earlier Jewish or Christian literature, including its distinctive legal corpus (inheritance law, ritual law, contract law), its specific theological formulations (e.g., the doctrine of tawhid as articulated in Surah 112), and its status in Islamic tradition as inimitable Arabic literary form (i'jaz al-Qur'an) — a claim about its own linguistic and structural originality, not its narrative content.

blocks.heading: Primary Source References
items: Surah 112 (Al-Ikhlas) — a concise, distinctly Qur'anic theological formula with no direct earlier parallel.

blocks.heading: Christian Apologetic Response
items: This is a real and fair line of inquiry, but it's worth applying evenhandedly: the Bible itself contains documented parallels to earlier Ancient Near Eastern literature (the flood narrative and the Epic of Gilgamesh, for instance), and Christian scholarship's standard response is that shared cultural material doesn't by itself determine a text's truth or divine origin — the same standard should be extended fairly when Islam's intertextuality is raised, rather than applying a double standard.

blocks.heading: Points for Respectful Discussion
items: Present this as a real scholarly research area with citable parallels, not as 'the Qur'an copied everything' — and be ready to address the same category of question about the Bible's own ANE literary context, since a well-prepared Muslim debater will raise it.

questions.title: What is the 'Satanic verses' incident, and do Muslim scholars accept it?

blocks.heading: Context
items: Early biographical literature (Ibn Ishaq via Ibn Hisham, Al-Tabari's History and Tafsir) reports that Muhammad once recited verses praising the Meccan goddesses al-Lat, al-Uzza, and Manat as intercessors ('these are the exalted cranes'), later retracting them as Satanic interpolation — an account explosive enough that both Muslim orthodoxy and Christian critics treat it with extreme care.

blocks.heading: Mainstream Position & Primary Sources
items: The majority classical and modern Sunni position rejects the story as inauthentic: its chains are weak (mursal/disconnected), it contradicts the doctrine of prophetic protection from such error ('isma), and exegetes like Ibn Kathir dismissed it outright. Modern scholars (e.g., Shahab Ahmed's detailed study) show the reports are early but argue they reflect later polemical storytelling, not history.

A minority of early authorities transmitted it, and Qur'an 22:52 ('Never did We send a messenger... but Satan threw [something] into his recitation') is read by critics as presupposing such an event — while mainstream tafsir reads 22:52 generally, of Satanic whispers or of abrogated wishes, not of this specific story.

Western critical scholars divide: some (Watt, early revisionists) treated it as too embarrassing to invent and thus likely historical; others note embarrassment-criteria cut both ways in polemical literature.

blocks.heading: Primary Source References
items: Ibn Ishaq, Sirat Rasul Allah (Ibn Hisham recension); Al-Tabari, History vol. 6 and Tafsir on 22:52.
Shahab Ahmed, 'Ibn Taymiyyah and the Satanic Verses' (academic analysis of the reports).

blocks.heading: Christian Apologetic Response
items: The honest apologetic rule here is restraint: since mainstream Islam itself rejects the story, pressing it as fact ('your prophet spoke for Satan') will be correctly dismissed as relying on weak reports — the very method this book forbids when hadith gradings are inconvenient.
